qualification: Cambridge International AS Level English Language 9093 (syllabus v2, examined 2024-2026)

items.prompt: Define discursive writing, and state the task’s terms.
items.canonical_answer: Discursive writing explores an issue from more than one side before reaching a view: the sides are given their room, and the reader is shown the reasoning that produces the conclusion. The task’s terms: it is one of the three Section B categories, set as 600–900 words and carrying twenty-five marks — and the wording of the particular question signals the variant it wants.
marking_guidance: Credit the meaning: exploring more than one side before reaching a view.
The task’s terms — one of three categories, 600–900 words, twenty-five marks — frame the definition.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.
objective_titles: Structure a discursive piece dialectically: a view, the opposing view, a reasoned resolution

items.prompt: Define argumentative writing.
items.canonical_answer: Argumentative writing argues for one position and answers the other side: the position is declared, defended with reasons and evidence, and the strongest case against is met rather than ignored. A reader of an argumentative piece is owed no mystery about where the writer stands — the arguing is the piece’s spine, from the first paragraph to the last.
marking_guidance: Credit the meaning: one position argued, with the other side answered.
The answered opposition is what separates arguing from merely asserting.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.
objective_titles: Structure a discursive piece dialectically: a view, the opposing view, a reasoned resolution

items.prompt: What distinguishes a discursive task from an argumentative one, and which wording signals which?
items.canonical_answer: A discursive task explores before it concludes: it owes the reader both sides at their strongest, and a view reached in front of them — signalled by "explore", "consider" and "both sides". An argumentative task argues from the first paragraph: it owes the reader one position held openly, and the other side answered rather than ignored — signalled by "argue", "make the case" and a named position. The difference is where the conclusion lives: built at the end of the exploration, or declared at the start and defended throughout — and both owe the reader fairness, because a reader who scents a stacked case stops weighing it.
marking_guidance: Must state the contrast: exploring to a view against arguing a position, with the signal wording named.
Must say what each owes the reader — strongest sides for one, an answered opposition for the other.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.
objective_titles: Structure a discursive piece dialectically: a view, the opposing view, a reasoned resolution

items.prompt: What is dialectical structure?
items.canonical_answer: Dialectical structure is thesis, antithesis, synthesis: the case stated, its strongest opposition voiced, and the reasoned view that survives the collision. The synthesis is not a compromise by default — it gives ground only where ground is owed, and holds the line where the case stands — which is what makes it a conclusion rather than a shrug.
marking_guidance: Credit the meaning: the three stages, named and in order.
The synthesis as a reasoned survivor, not an automatic middle, is the definition’s centre.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.
objective_titles: Structure a discursive piece dialectically: a view, the opposing view, a reasoned resolution

items.prompt: Give the steps for planning a dialectical piece.
items.canonical_answer: First write the thesis in one sentence — the case the piece is for. Second write the antithesis at its strongest: the best version of the case against, not the easiest to beat. Third mark the concession: what the antithesis has right, and the piece will admit. Fourth draft the synthesis: the view that survives, giving the conceded ground and holding the rest. Then plan the sections against those four lines, and every paragraph has a place in the argument.
marking_guidance: Credit the steps in order: thesis, strongest antithesis, concession, synthesis.
The antithesis at its strongest is the step that decides whether the synthesis is worth having.

objective_titles: Structure a discursive piece dialectically: a view, the opposing view, a reasoned resolution

items.prompt: Name the four forms the discursive/argumentative question takes, with one convention of each.
items.canonical_answer: The article, for a magazine or newspaper’s readership — it carries a headline, subheadings and a register that welcomes the browser. The essay, for a class or a prose publication — continuous, unheaded, its structure carried entirely by its paragraphs. The speech, for a hall — it addresses its audience directly, signposts its route, repeats for listeners and closes on its ask. The letter to an editor, for a paper’s readership through its editor — it salutes, quotes the claim it answers and signs off.
marking_guidance: Credit the four forms with a convention each: the article’s subheadings, the essay’s continuity, the speech’s address and ask, the letter’s salutation and sign-off.
Each convention belongs to its form, so a list of forms without conventions has named half the card.

objective_titles: Structure a discursive piece dialectically: a view, the opposing view, a reasoned resolution

items.prompt: A piece titled "Is technology making us lonely?" gives five paragraphs of reasons that it is, and closes: "So the answer is yes." What has gone wrong, and what does the reader who disagreed take away?
items.canonical_answer: What has gone wrong is the argument that never happened: five paragraphs of one side, no counterargument voiced, and a one-line conclusion dropped on the reader like a gavel. The reader who disagreed takes away exactly what they brought — their objection, unmet and unweakened — because the piece never once stood in their shoes, and the table rewards the task achieved, which includes the other side. The fix is the dialectical plan: the antithesis given its strongest paragraph before the synthesis earns its say.
marking_guidance: Must name the mistake: one side listed, the other never met, a conclusion instead of an argument.
Must say what the disagreeing reader takes away — their objection intact — and give the dialectical fix.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.
objective_titles: Structure a discursive piece dialectically: a view, the opposing view, a reasoned resolution

items.prompt: A task sets an essay on "modern life and what it costs". The writer covers phones, work, food, travel, friendships, reading, weather and politics — one paragraph each. What has gone wrong, and what is the cure?
items.canonical_answer: The error is the scope never narrowed: the wording names a whole civilisation, and the piece takes it all on, which thins every paragraph to a page of headlines — eight subjects, eight undeveloped. The cure is to choose one part and let the whole be visible behind it: an essay about what phones did to the family dinner is an essay about modern life, and its six paragraphs can carry reasons, examples and a view. Scope is chosen, not inherited: the task names the country, and the writing picks the street.
marking_guidance: Must name the mistake: the whole issue taken on, so every section is thinned.
Must give the cure: one part chosen, the whole visible behind it — the country named, the street picked.

objective_titles: Structure a discursive piece dialectically: a view, the opposing view, a reasoned resolution

items.prompt: A task sets an essay. The learner submits a magazine article, complete with a headline and four subheadings. What has gone wrong, and why does it matter to the marks?
items.canonical_answer: The error is the wrong form: the task named an essay, and the essay’s conventions — continuous prose, no headline, no subheadings, structure carried by its paragraphs — are part of its brief. It matters because the form is named in the task, and the table rewards the task achieved in full: a piece that would have earned its marks as an article is marked as a poorer fit as an essay, however well written, because it has shown the wrong kind of writing. The fix is one word: reread the form named, and write that.
marking_guidance: Must name the mistake: an article’s conventions where an essay’s were set.
Must say why it costs: the form is part of the task, so the piece is marked as a poorer fit.

items.prompt: Define a counterargument.
items.canonical_answer: A counterargument is the position that opposes yours: the best case that can be made for the other side, in its strongest form. In an argument it is voiced fairly — because a case that meets only weak objections has met none — and it is the writer’s job to give it its full weight before answering it.
marking_guidance: Credit the meaning: the opposing position, at its strongest.
The fairness of voicing it well is part of the definition’s use.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.
objective_titles: Set counterarguments beside your points and answer them

items.prompt: What does placing a counterargument beside your point do for the argument?
items.canonical_answer: It makes the argument stronger, because the reader watches the case survive its strongest test: the objection is voiced where the case is at full strength, answered in the same room, and the reader who held it feels met rather than managed. An objection answered in a clause is an objection being hidden, and the reader knows it — the full paragraph, fairly voiced, is the argument’s badge of confidence.
marking_guidance: Credit the meaning: the objection met at full strength, in the same room as the case.
What it does for the reader — met rather than managed — is the definition’s effect.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.
objective_titles: Set counterarguments beside your points and answer them

items.prompt: Read this pair of sentences, written for the purpose: "It is true that the new road will take the old trees, and the old trees matter. It is also true that the flooding the road prevents will take more of them, root and bank." How does the concession-rebuttal sequence work on the reader?
items.canonical_answer: The concession pays the objection its due — the trees matter, said plainly, before any answer — which earns the trust the rebuttal then spends: the reader who loved the trees has been met, and is given a reason to weigh rather than a verdict to resist. The mechanism is the admission: by conceding first, the writer shows the case has been tested and survived its own honesty, so the rebuttal’s arithmetic — more trees lost to the flood than to the road — lands as fairness rather than spin, and the reader is recruited into the weighing.
marking_guidance: Must name the mechanism in the sentences’ words: the concession earning the trust the rebuttal spends.
Must trace the effect on the reader: met, then given something to weigh, which is how the objection is disarmed.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.
objective_titles: Set counterarguments beside your points and answer them

items.prompt: Here is a counterargument: "Later school starts simply shuffle the problem: the teenagers will just stay up later, and learn the same lesson later." Write a concession-and-rebutter sentence in reply.
items.canonical_answer: A model reply: "It is true that some learners will spend a later start on a later night — the body clock is an invitation, not a law — and yet the melatonin evidence is about the sleep the body will accept, not the nights it is offered: a start moved to eight gives the teenager two more hours of the sleep their body is already begging for, and the ones who waste it will at least waste it awake, on time." (Any sentence that concedes the real part of the objection — the shuffle — and then answers what remains does the job: the admission first, the answer second.)
marking_guidance: Credit the reply as a piece of text: a concession that names what is right in the objection, then the rebutter to what remains.
The strongest answers concede the weaker part and answer the decisive part, so the reader watches the case hold.

items.prompt: Here is an argument paragraph, written for the purpose: "Recycling is pointless. Our town’s blue bins end up in the same landfill as everything else — my neighbour saw the trucks. Until the system is honest, sorting your rubbish is theatre." How convincing is the paragraph, and what does it overlook?
items.canonical_answer: The paragraph has force: it opens on a claim, gives evidence (the neighbour’s trucks) and lands a memorable verdict ("theatre"). But its conviction rests on one unchecked anecdote, and what it overlooks decides the judgement: the town’s published waste figures, which any argument about the system would need; the difference between one collection route and the whole system; and the logical leap from "the system is dishonest" to "sorting is pointless", which only follows if the dishonesty is total and permanent. However, its core challenge — that recycling theatre without honesty deserves the name — is a real one, and a stronger paragraph would keep it: the judgement is persuasive about the problem and unconvincing about the conclusion, because the evidence does not reach it.
marking_guidance: Credit the judgement: forceful but unconvincing, with reasons drawn from what it overlooks.
Credit the case for its strength, however: the anecdote’s appeal and the verdict’s memorability, because a fair evaluation weighs both sides.
The strongest answers name the missing evidence the conclusion needed — the published figures — which is the omission that defeats it.

items.prompt: A paragraph argues: "Homework is stressful. Stress is harmful. Homework causes harm, and harm is what stress from homework does." What is the paragraph doing, and what has it not done?
items.canonical_answer: The paragraph is repeating in argument’s clothing: three sentences that restate one claim — homework causes stress — and no sentence that adds reason, example or consequence. What it has not done is develop: who is stressed, how much, compared with what, and what follows — the evidence that would turn a claim into a case. The addition test catches it: what did the third sentence add? Only phrasing, and the paragraph’s development is still owed.
marking_guidance: Must name the mistake: repetition dressed as development, with nothing added.
Must give the addition test and the questions the paragraph still owes — who, how much, compared with what.

items.prompt: Here is a sentence, written for the purpose: "We asked for a queue, and we were given a form; we asked for a form, and we were given a committee; we asked for a committee, and here we are." How do the tricolon and the anaphora add force to the argument?
items.canonical_answer: The anaphora — "we asked… and we were given" three times — turns three separate disappointments into a single pressure the reader feels as a pattern, and the tricolon completes the thought with a beat the reader can agree to: the third item lands the joke and the verdict together ("and here we are"). The force is rhythmic: the reader who might argue with one complaint has been given three in one breath, shaped so each makes the next worse — and the inclusive "we" has already made the reader a member of the asking, so agreeing with the beat feels like remembering rather than deciding.
marking_guidance: Must name the devices in the sentence’s words: the anaphora of the asking, the tricolon’s closing beat.
Must trace how the force works: pattern as pressure, and the reader recruited by the "we" into agreement.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.
objective_titles: Use rhetorical devices with control to persuade a named audience

items.prompt: A speech to a youth forum contains this sentence: "Every one of us has stood in a queue that our parents built and been handed a form that our grandparents designed." How does the inclusive pronoun work on this audience?
items.canonical_answer: The inclusive pronoun — "every one of us", "our" twice — makes the audience members of the case rather than its targets: the queue and the form are a shared inheritance, and the young audience is told they are already in the story, on the speaker’s side, before any proposal arrives. The mechanism is membership: a reader who is "we" argues about what to do, while a reader who is "you" argues about whether to listen — and the sentence has chosen the first argument, which is the one a persuader wants to be having.
marking_guidance: Must name the mechanism in the sentence’s words: the inclusive pronoun building membership rather than targeting.
Must trace the effect: the audience argues about what to do instead of whether to listen — the argument the speaker wants.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.
objective_titles: Use rhetorical devices with control to persuade a named audience

items.prompt: What is the difference between persuasive force and a ranting tone, and what happens to the reader of each?
items.canonical_answer: Persuasive force argues the case: evidence, concession, rebuttal, and a tone that invites the reader to weigh. A rant relieves the writer: accusation, repetition, and a tone that tells the reader what to feel. The reader of force weighs and is recruited; the reader of a rant defends themselves — checking the case for faults instead of weighing it — and the audience the piece was written to hold becomes the audience the piece has attacked. The line between them is often the second person: "you have ignored" accuses, and "we have not yet asked" recruits.
marking_guidance: Must state the contrast: arguing the case against relieving the writer.
Must say what happens to each reader: recruited by the first, self-defending and lost by the second.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.
objective_titles: Use rhetorical devices with control to persuade a named audience

items.prompt: Here is an accusing sentence: "People like you have never cared what happens to the river — you dump, you pollute, you look away." Rewrite it in a measured, persuasive register, keeping the complaint.
items.canonical_answer: A rewrite: "The river has carried everything we have chosen not to name — the dumping we have watched, the pollution we have priced, and the looking away that all of us, at one time or another, have found convenient. What we have not yet done is ask what it would cost to stop." (Any version that keeps the complaint, drops the accusation and recruits the reader into the "we" does the job: the measured register argues rather than relieves.)
marking_guidance: Credit the rewrite: the complaint kept in a measured register, because the words are the proof.
The strongest answers move from "you" to "we" and keep the evidence, so the reader is recruited rather than accused.

items.prompt: A learner argues well for three paragraphs and then writes a fourth that begins: "And frankly, anyone who disagrees is either stupid or being paid." What has happened, and what does the fourth paragraph cost?
items.canonical_answer: The tone has slid into ranting: the fourth paragraph relieves the writer instead of arguing the case, and its cost is the three good paragraphs, because the reader who was weighing the argument is now being told what to think of them by a writer who has stopped trusting the evidence. The audience the piece was written to hold — including the readers who disagreed politely — is told they are stupid or corrupt, and they leave; the piece ends with a smaller room than it started with. The fix is deletion: the fourth paragraph is not an argument but a sigh, and the third paragraph was the ending.
marking_guidance: Must name the mistake: the rant that replaces argument with insult.
Must say what it costs: the audience lost, including the politely disagreeing readers the case needed.

items.prompt: Write an essay for a class discussion, giving your view on whether homework should be abolished. Explore the strongest case on both sides before reaching your view. Use 600–900 words. [25]
items.canonical_answer:
Should homework be abolished? The honest answer is that homework is not one thing, and the question deserves better than a banner.
Let me begin with what works, because a case that starts with concessions is a case you can trust. Homework done well is practice, and practice consolidates: the learner who writes the spelling list out twice on Tuesday will remember it on Friday, not because writing is magical but because memory is a muscle and Friday is a test of it. Our own class ran a two-week experiment last term — half the list practised at home, half not — and the practised half scored, on average, thirty per cent higher. That is not a policy. That is a fact, and a fact this essay will not pretend away.
And yet the case against homework is not the case against practice — it is the case against what homework actually measures. Homework measures the home. The learner with the quiet room, the desk, the parent home by six and the data bundle that reaches the school’s portal is doing one exercise; the learner with the shift-working parent, the shared room and the bundle that ran out on Tuesday is doing another, and the difference is invisible on the worksheet and decisive on the mark. When our class ran our two-week experiment, the thirty per cent gain was not shared evenly: it arrived almost entirely among the quiet-roomed half. Practice consolidates for the learners who can practise. For the rest, the same worksheet does not consolidate — it humbles.
So the abolition argument has real force: if the set task measures the home and not the learner, the set task is not assessment but assumption. I want to concede that fully, because the argument deserves it. And yet abolishing practice does not fix the inequality — it removes the practice from the learners it serves and the humiliation from the learners it harms, and calls the removal a reform. The thirty per cent still exists; it is simply no longer anyone’s to give.
Here is the view I think survives: abolish the homework that measures homes, keep the homework that consolidates, and know the difference. Set it shorter — fifteen minutes, not an hour — so the shift-working parent is not the deciding variable. Set it smarter — practice, not projects, because projects are where the home shows. And let the school day carry the rest: the supervised prep period our school piloted last year moved the practice inside the walls, where the quiet room is everyone’s. It is not a banner, and it will not fit on one. But the question deserved better than a banner, and so — if we are honest — do the learners.
There is one more thing the essay owes, and it is the teacher’s view. Homework is the only hour of the school week that the teacher sees through glass: set on Monday, returned on Friday, the middle invisible. When it works, the teacher never knows why; when it fails, the failure arrives without its story. The reform I am proposing — shorter, fairer, set inside walls where the walls belong to everyone — is not only a reform of the worksheet. It is a reform of the seeing: the supervised prep period returns the middle of the task to the room where the teacher stands in it, and the thirty per cent stops being a surprise to everyone, including the people who earned it.
Homework is not one thing. Practised fairly, it is the memory’s friend; practised blindly, it is inequality with a due date. The reform is not to abolish it but to make it fair — and we are the ones holding the pen that sets it.

items.prompt: Write a magazine article exploring whether social media has made friendships stronger or weaker. Give both sides their strongest case before reaching your view. Use 600–900 words. [25]
items.canonical_answer:
Is social media making friendships weaker? The evidence says it changed the currency, not the worth.
I will make the case against first, and I will make it properly, because I held it myself for years. The friendships of my parents’ generation had weather in them: you walked to your friend’s house, and if the friend was out, the walk was wasted, so you learned to arrange, to commit, to turn up. Social media removed the turning up. The group chat replaces the visit; the birthday message replaces the birthday; ‘we should catch up’ becomes a genre of message that both parties know means the opposite. The phrase-talk is real — I have friends whose entire friendship is liking each other’s photographs — and the friend who was reachable is now only contactable, which is a different and thinner thing.
That is the case against, and I am not going to insult it by answering a weaker version. So here is what it overlooks. It overlooks the friend found again after twenty years, because the platforms are also the lost-and-found of the species: my mother’s childhood friend, traced through two towns and a surname change, is now back in her life on a Sunday call. It overlooks the group chat that organised a funeral in three days — forty relatives, one message thread, and a family that functioned in its worst week because it had a room to meet in. And it overlooks the ordinary Tuesday: my closest friendship survives a two-hour time difference on a ten-minute call that would once have been a letter and, before that, silence.
So which is it — thinner or stronger? I think it is both, and the honest answer is about currency. Contact got cheaper, and presence got rarer. When a message costs nothing, the message proves nothing — the old friendship’s proofs are gone. But when presence is possible at a distance, the presence is chosen, and chosen presence is the strongest proof there is: the friend who calls on a Tuesday, when a like would have done, is choosing the expensive version of the friendship. The friendships that matter are learning to spend both — cheap contact to keep the thread, and rare presence to keep the worth.
And the currency metaphor earns one more paragraph, because it explains something the case against never quite does. My parents’ friendships were strong partly because they had to be: the cost of contact made every contact an investment, and the investment built the worth. We are the first generation that can hold a friendship at almost no cost, and the discovery we are making — slowly, badly, on our phones, in our group chats — is what the worth was made of all along. It was never the cost. It was the choosing. The platforms made choosing cheap, and our job is to keep choosing expensively anyway: to send the message and then also make the call, to close the app and open the door, to arrive, sometimes, in person, at a house, with the weather still in us.
The worry I keep, and I will end with it: the cheap contact can pass for the presence, and the platform is designed to help it pass. The friendship that lives on likes is a currency that looks like wealth and spends like paper. The tool will not fix that. We will — by calling, sometimes, on Tuesdays, at a cost. It is a small discipline for a large thing: the worth of a friendship was never in the watermark of its messages, and every generation has had to decide what its own version of showing up would be. Ours gets to choose both.

items.prompt: Write a speech to a youth forum, arguing for or against a ban on single-use plastics. Make the case for your position and answer the strongest case against it. Use 600–900 words. [25]
items.canonical_answer:
Fellow delegates — I stand to argue that this forum should support a ban on single-use plastics, and I want to begin by admitting the strongest case against me.
The case against the ban is the case for the ordinary person’s Tuesday. The single-use plastic in question — the packet, the cup, the sachet — is the cheapest clean packaging humanity has ever made, and the ban that removes it removes it first from the Tuesday of the person with the least: the water sachet is the cold drink of the street, the packet is the portion that fits the smallest budget, and telling that person to carry a reusable cup is telling them to buy a cup. A ban written by people with cupboards lands on people without them. I have heard this argument made well, and I will not make it badly so I can beat it.
And here is my answer. The sachet is cheap at the till and expensive at the drain — the cost has not gone away, it has moved: to the river, the landfill’s six-hundred-year half-life, the blockage that floods the street in the rainy season and the livestock that cannot read the word ‘disposable’. The cheapest packaging humanity ever made is being paid for by the people who can least afford it, in the one currency they cannot refuse — their own water, their own streets, their own soil. We, the generation that inherits the bill, are the cheapest thing the sachet’s makers never priced.
So I am not asking for a ban that lands on Tuesdays. I am asking this forum to support a ban that begins where the choice is not the sachet but the system: the supermarket wrap before the street sachet, the manufacturer before the buyer, the supply that decides the demand. Let the street keep the cold drink — and let the cold drink arrive in something the drain can forgive. A ban phased in from the top of the chain is a ban the Tuesday can survive, and even afford.
Let me answer the second objection too, because it is already in the room: the ban does not work, the bans elsewhere leaked, the shops sold out of stockpiles, the river was no cleaner a year on. It is true. It is also an argument against badly written bans, which is what we will write badly if we write them in a hurry and alone. A ban phased in over years, with the sachet’s replacement designed before the sachet’s funeral, enforced by the generation that will drink from the river longest — that ban has not been tried here, and the failure of a different ban in a different hurry is not a prophecy of ours. We are allowed to learn from other people’s mistakes instead of inheriting them.
Because here is the thing about my generation and the sachet: we are not the first to drink from it, but we will be the ones to bury it — the packets outlive the water, the cup outlives the drinker, and a hundred years from now, someone digging in our landfill will be able to date our town by its plastics. We are asking for the right to leave less of ourselves behind. Support the ban, phase it fairly, start at the top of the chain — and drink to a Tuesday our grandchildren can dig up without recognising. I ask the forum for its vote, I ask the delegates for their questions, and I ask the sachet’s makers to start counting the drain the way this town already does.

items.prompt: Write a letter to a newspaper, responding to a proposal to close the public library and replace it with a digital hub. Argue your position and answer the proposal’s strongest points. Use 600–900 words. [25]
items.canonical_answer:
Dear Editor,
Your correspondent of last week supports the council’s proposal to close the public library and move its books to a ‘digital hub’ in the municipal building. I write to answer the proposal, because I have counted what it costs and what it claims to save.
The claim is savings, and I concede the arithmetic at once: the library building costs the council rates money — the roof is old, the lights are many, and the figures quoted are real. I have no quarrel with the sums. My quarrel is with what the sums leave out.
They leave out the forty-one learners who used the library last Tuesday between three and six — I counted them, with the librarian’s permission, on the wettest afternoon of the month. They leave out the six-week waiting list for the three most popular series, which is not a statistic about books but a statistic about readers being made, one waiting list at a time. They leave out the study desk that a learner without a quiet room at home calls, in the words of one of them I will not attribute, ‘the only place I get anything done’. A digital hub replaces the books and keeps none of this. The books are the cheapest thing in the building.
And it must be said plainly that ‘digital’ is not the neutral word the proposal treats it as. The hub requires a device, a data bundle and a home to plug them into — the reader with all three is well served by the future, and the reader without them is not served at all, and the proposal’s own figures for household connectivity in this town are published. Closing the building to fund the hub is moving the library into the homes that can afford to house it. We are proposing to means-test a public good.
There is a version of the future I would support: the library with a hub inside it — the wiring renewed, the roof paid for by the rates increase we were all told was coming anyway, and the books kept exactly where the waiting list can reach them. The council’s own survey, published with the proposal, found that sixty-two per cent of respondents wanted the building kept and modernised, which the proposal’s summary, published with the same survey, described as ‘mixed’.
And to the readers who are weighing the proposal honestly, I offer one number more, because the case is not only about readers. The library’s budget, published in the same council papers, is 3.1 per cent of the proposal’s own cost estimate for the hub — the wiring, the devices, the subscriptions and the staff are the expensive parts, and the roof was due its re-thatching in the maintenance plan of 2024, which the papers also contain. The savings the proposal advertises are the difference between a building we chose to maintain and a building we chose not to. That is a choice, and choices can be made differently, and the twelfth is the day for making it.
I ask your readers to write to the consultation before the twelfth, and to say the thing the survey already said: a town that is closing its library to build its future has mistaken the library for the past. The library is where the future learns to read — and the town that keeps it open is choosing, at the price of a re-thatched roof, to keep the door of that future on the latch for everyone, not only for the homes with the wiring for a hub. That is a choice worth the rates increase we were told was coming anyway.
Yours faithfully,
A. Katjaviva, library user since 1998

items.prompt: Define a concession.
items.canonical_answer: A concession is the part of the counterargument you admit is right before you answer the rest: the ground given honestly, so that the reply is trusted. "It is true that the new road will take the old trees" concedes before it answers — and the admission earns the trust the rebuttal spends, which is why an argument that concedes nothing convinces nobody.
marking_guidance: Credit the meaning: the part of the opposing case admitted before answering the rest.
What the concession earns — trust for the reply — is the definition’s purpose.
